name: Embedded AI Engineering
tagline: Make machine learning run on tiny, power-sipping chips.
description: From bits, volts and your first C program to the systems that run neural networks on microcontrollers, phones and custom chips: embedded systems, signal processing, deep learning, model compression, ML compilers and accelerators, up to today's research on efficient AI. It follows the syllabi of leading university courses and the field's standard books.
notation: kB = 1,000 bytes and KiB = 1,024 bytes (likewise MB/MiB); b is a bit, B a byte.
One MAC (multiply-accumulate) counts as 2 FLOPs (or 2 integer ops).
Tensors are NCHW or NHWC (batch, channels, height, width); a convolution kernel is K×K unless a paper's R×S notation is quoted.
Matrix multiply: an M×K matrix times a K×N matrix costs M·N·K MACs.
Quantization: r = S(q − Z) with scale S and zero-point Z; int8 spans [−128, 127], uint8 [0, 255].
Floating-point formats: FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8 E4M3 and E5M2; block formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4.
C is C11/C17 with <stdint.h> types; assume 32-bit int and little-endian unless a card says otherwise.
Energy in pJ per operation, power in mW, latency in ms, throughput in inferences/s or TOPS.
Big-O describes growth in the input size n, as in computer science.

Energy figures from Horowitz (ISSCC 2014, 45 nm) are quoted per 32-bit operation: int add 0.1 pJ, float add 0.9 pJ, int multiply 3.1 pJ, float multiply 3.7 pJ, SRAM read about 5 pJ from 8 KB and about 10 pJ from 32 KB, DRAM read about 640 pJ.
